question: What is an example of a condition where orbital exenteration would be an appropriate initial management?

options.B: Merkel cell carcinoma of the eyelid
options.D: extraocular extension of choroidal melanoma in a patient with lung metastasis

explanation: Exenteration is an extensive surgical procedure deﬁned by removal of the soft tissue contents of the orbit. A subtotal exenteration is basically an enucleation with removal of the adjacent lesion, leaving the periorbita and most or all of the eyelids. In a total exenteration, all intraorbital soft tissue is removed, usually including the eyelids. An extended exenteration involves removal of all orbital soft tissue, as well as adjacent bony structures, such as the paranasal sinuses and/or the skull BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: A 25-year-old man who admits to intravenous (IV) drug use has a lesion on the left upper and lower lid (Figure 1). What additional diagnostic testing is most important for this patient?
explanation: The mass depicted is a Kaposi sarcoma. It presents as a reddish dermal mass and is a frequent manifestation of AIDS. These lesions are associated with human herpesvirus 8. In addition to the eyelid manifestations, conjunctival lesions can also present and appear similar to foreign body granulomas or cavernous hemangiomas. Histologically, they are composed of spindle cells. Treatment can include cryotherapy, excision, radiation, or intralesional chemotherapeutic agents. Often, these lesions can regress following immune reconstitution with adequate antiviral treatment of the HIV infection.

question: A 70-year-old patient presents with a chronic chalazion, asymmetric eyelid inﬂammation, and loss of normal adnexal structures. What is the preferred next step in management?
explanation: This description is suspicious for sebaceous adenocarcinoma (ﬁgure). Full-thickness eyelid biopsy is indicated to avoid sampling only superﬁcial inﬂammatory change overlying a potentially malignant lesion. Conjunctival map biopsies are helpful to deﬁne the extent of the process. A superﬁcial biopsy can miss the underlying pathology. Radiation and cryotherapy are not indicated without a tissue diagnosis.

question: What is the cell most likely to act as both target and eﬀector in Graves ophthalmopathy?
explanation: Orbital ﬁbroblasts are embryologically derived from the neural crest and possess developmental plasticity. They express CD40 receptors, generally found on B cells. When engaged by T-cell- bound CD154, ﬁbroblast proinﬂammatory cytokines, such as interleukin-6 (IL-6), IL-8, and prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), are upregulated, which in turn increases the synthesis of hyaluronan and glycosaminoglycan (GAG). Circulating immunoglobulin (IgG) may also stimulate orbital ﬁbroblasts to secrete GAG and other cytokines that trigger orbital inﬂammation. Furthermore, signaling through thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor (TSH-R) on orbital ﬁbroblasts may promote adipogenesis, thereby stimulating the expansion of the orbital fat compartments seen in patients with Graves ophthalmopathy. &

question: A patient has sustained a full- thickness laceration to the central lower eyelid that involves the margin. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: realignment of the tarsus with partial-thickness sutures and eversion of the eyelid margin with vertical mattress sutures
options.B: realignment of the tarsus with full-thickness sutures and eversion of the eyelid margin with vertical mattress sutures
options.C: realignment of the tarsus with partial-thickness sutures and ﬂush realignment of the eyelid margin with vertical mattress sutures
options.D: realignment of the tarsus with full-thickness sutures and ﬂush realignment of the eyelid margin with vertical mattress sutures

explanation: Full-thickness lacerations involving the eyelid margin require repair of the tarsal plate, with attention to the lid margin to prevent formation of a notch. The tarsus is reapproximated with partial-thickness sutures, because full-thickness tarsal sutures would typically cause a corneal abrasion. The tails of the partial-thickness sutures should also be directed anteriorly. The lid margin is best approximated with a vertical mattress suture. question: Where is the valve of Hasner located? realignment of the tarsus with full-thickness sutures and eversion of the eyelid margin with vertical mattress sutures B. 10 Your Answer realignment of the tarsus with partial-thickness sutures and ﬂush realignment of the eyelid margin with vertical mattress sutures C.
explanation: The valve of Hasner is located at the distal end of the nasolacrimal duct. It represents a mucosal ﬂap over the distal ostium of the nasolacrimal duct (NLD) below the inferior turbinate of the nose. The persistent membrane at the valve of Hasner is a common site of congenital NLD obstruction. The junction of the common canaliculus and lacrimal sac represents the valve of Rosenmüller.

question: A 65-year-old female presents with a history of blunt trauma to the left orbit one week ago. She reports immediate onset of binocular vertical diplopia, which has improved since onset. Examination shows a left hypertropia that worsens on downgaze associated with limitation of infraduction of the left eye. Forced ductions were negative. Coronal computed tomography (CT) shows a non- displaced inferior orbital ﬂoor fracture. What is the appropriate next step in management?

options.C: Botulinum toxin to the left superior rectus muscle

explanation: The patient's history is most consistent with left inferior rectus muscle contusion/edema based on her left hypertropia worsening on downgaze with gradual improvement since onset. There is no evidence of inferior rectus muscle entrapment (which would usually cause a right hypertropia worsening on attempted upgaze, due to limited supraduction of the left eye). The patient reports spontaneous improvement within 1 week; therefore, neither surgical exploration nor strabismus surgery is indicated. Botulinum toxin is not recommended, as her diplopia would be anticipated to resolve spontaneously within 1-2 weeks and botulinum toxin will last, on average, for 3-4 months.

question: What is the most common site for metastasis to the orbit?
explanation: In adults, the most common metastatic tumors to the orbit are from the breast and lung. Signs of metastasis to the orbit include pain, proptosis, inﬂammation, bone destruction, and early ophthalmoplegia. The most common site for metastasis is the extraocular muscles because of their abundant vascular supply. The bone marrow space of the sphenoid bone is the second most common site of metastasis because of the high volume of low-ﬂow blood in this area. &

question: A 78-year-old man develops a desensitized cornea and lagophthalmos following a stroke. After managing his lagophthalmos for 6 months with copious lubrication and taping closed his eyelids, what would be the preferred surgical treatment to avoid corneal ulceration?
explanation: Poor blinking and eyelid closure secondary to CN VII injury can lead to chronic ocular surface irritation from corneal exposure, as well as poor tear ﬁlm replenishment and distribution. Lubricating drops, viscous tear supplementation, ointments, taping of the temporal half of the lower eyelid, or moisture chambers may be used alone or in combination for temporary paralysis. For cases of long-term or permanent paralysis of the eyelid, additional procedures are necessary. Placement of a weight in the upper eyelid remains the most commonly performed procedure for the treatment of paralytic lagophthalmos. Although a complete tarsorrhaphy will reduce corneal exposure, patients dislike the permanent tarsorrhaphy from a functional and cosmetic perspective. This procedure should be avoided, except in patients with recalcitrant corneal disease from exposure. A Müller muscle resection would cause worsening of symptoms with more upper lid retraction and exposure of the ocular surface, and it is not indicated for this patient with lagophthalmos. Eyelid springs have less long-term success and greater risk of extrusion.

question: A 10-year-old boy is struck in the left eye with a baseball and arrives to the emergency room vomiting 3 hours after the injury. An ophthalmologist is consulted because the boy is complaining of diplopia. On examination, visual acuity is 20/20 in each eye. Motility shows an inability to supraduct the left eye but is otherwise full. He has extreme pain with attempted upgaze. Both eyes appear white and quiet. What is the most likely etiology of the patient’s vomiting?
explanation: The patient presents with a white-eyed blowout fracture on the left side. Patients typically present with a white, quiet eye with an inability to supraduct the involved eye because the inferior rectus muscle is trapped within the fractured inferior orbital wall.

question: A patient undergoes a retrobulbar anesthetic injection just prior to glaucoma ﬁltering surgery. What change in eye position is the surgeon likely to observe intraoperatively?

options.B: incyclotorsion and depression of the eye
options.C: excyclotorsion and elevation of the eye

explanation: A retrobulbar injection introduces anesthetic into the intraconal space, an extension of the fascial planes of the annulus of Zinn. The annulus of Zinn is formed by the 4 rectus muscle insertions and their intermuscular fascia; it encompasses the optic canal and splits the superior orbital ﬁssure into an intraconal and extraconal compartment (Figure 1). The intraconal compartment contains both divisions of the oculomotor (III) and abducens (VI) nerves. Also recall that the nerve to the inferior oblique muscle travels in the inferior branch of the oculomotor nerve. Therefore, abduction, supraduction, and excyclotorsion would not occur, as these motor nerves have been anesthetized by the retrobulbar block. The trochlear nerve (IV) lies outside the annulus of Zinn in the extraconal space, and is often spared during retrobulbar blocks, resulting in intact incyclotorsion and infraduction of the globe intraoperatively. question: What procedure would best correct a deep superior sulcus deformity following evisceration?

options.B: replacing prosthesis with a smaller prosthesis
options.C: subperiosteal secondary implant on the orbital ﬂoor
options.D: dermis-fat graft to the upper lid

explanation: A deep superior sulcus is a common deformity following evisceration or enucleation; it is best corrected by placement of a subperiosteal secondary implant on the orbital ﬂoor. This implant pushes the initial implant and superior orbital fat upward to ﬁll out the superior sulcus. Dermis-fat grafts may be implanted to the upper eyelid to ﬁll out the sulcus, but eyelid contour and function may be damaged, and the graft may undergo resorption.

question: What procedure that is used to correct punctal ectropion involves a horizontal fusiform excision of conjunctiva and eyelid retractors 4 mm inferior to the puncta?
explanation: In cases of mild medial ectropion with punctal eversion, a medial spindle procedure can be performed. The procedure involves a horizontal fusiform excision of conjunctiva and eyelid retractors 4 mm inferior to the puncta, followed by inverting sutures for closure. In cases with associated horizontal eyelid laxity, lateral canthal tightening may be used in conjunction with this procedure. In the lateral tarsal strip procedure, the tarsus is sutured directly to the lateral orbital rim periosteum. The goal of this procedure is to correct the position of the eyelid while maintaining the horizontal dimension of the palpebral ﬁssure and a sharp, correctly positioned lateral canthal angle. Punctoplasty changes the size of the puncta and does not alter the punctal position relative to the globe. Rotational suture techniques are used as temporizing measures for involutional entropion; however, when these techniques are used in isolation, recurrence is anticipated.

question: What is the most common histopathologic type of rhabdomyosarcoma?
explanation: Rhabdomyosarcoma (ﬁgure) is the most common primary pediatric malignancy of the orbit. The average age of presentation is 5 to 7 years, usually with proptosis, globe displacement, ptosis, conjunctival and eyelid swelling, and pain. Usually, the onset is rapid, and suspicion of rhabdomyosarcoma should prompt urgent workup in any young child with these ﬁndings. After imaging studies reveal the location and extent of the tumor, a biopsy should be done, along with an evaluation for metastases. The ﬁgure shows: A. Child with a large orbital mass. B. CT scan (axial view) showing a large, poorly circumscribed orbital tumor. C. The neoplastic cells tend to diﬀerentiate toward muscle cells. In this moderately diﬀerentiated embryonal example, cross- striations representing Z-bands of actin-myosin complexes within the cytoplasm can be easily identiﬁed. It is common for these cells to be more primitive, with a featureless abundant cytoplasm. In the less-diﬀerentiated cases, electron microscopy and immunohistochemistry may be necessary to correctly identify the neoplasm. D. Poorly cohesive rhabdomyoblasts separated by ﬁbrous septa into “alveoli” are low-magniﬁcation histologic features of the alveolar variant of rhabdomyosarcoma. This variant may have a less favorable natural history than the more common embryonal type. Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common subtype, accounting for 80% of cases, with sheets of poorly diﬀerentiated malignant cells showing few cross-striations. Alveolar diﬀerentiation accounts for 9% of cases and is the most malignant form. It shows ﬁbrovascular strands with rounded rhabdomyoblasts along the strands or freely ﬂoating in alveolar spaces. Pleomorphic is the least common and most diﬀerentiated with easily visualized cross-striations. Botryoid variants are rare in the orbit but may arise and invade from the conjunctiva or paranasal sinuses. The rhabdomyosarcoma cells are thought to originate from undiﬀerentiated orbital mesenchymal cells rather than from the extraocular muscles. Smaller tumors are excised while larger tumors require chemotherapy and radiation. The 5-year survival rate is 94% with BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: A 24-year-old woman is referred for evaluation of the clinical ﬁnding seen in the ﬁgure. It has been present since birth. What condition is this patient at increased risk of developing?
explanation: The patient described has oculodermal melanocytosis, also known as nevus of Ota. Although malignant transformation may occur, especially in white patients, no prophylactic treatment is recommended. Ten percent (10%) of patients with oculodermal melanocytosis also have glaucoma and pigmentation of the trabecular meshwork. There is no relationship with this condition to cataract formation. Multiple eyelid lentigines, which are ﬂat, pigmented spots larger than ephelides, may be associated with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, which is associated with intestinal polyposis, with increased risk of colon cancer. Approximately 0.25% of patients with oculodermal melanocytosis develop a uveal melanoma, but there is no known relationship to the development of uveitis.

question: A 35-year-old woman complains of drooping of her eyelids. She reports several previous episodes of intermittent painless swelling of her eyelids. Her ﬁndings at presentation are shown in the ﬁgure. What diagnosis is most likely?
explanation: Blepharochalasis is a rare condition that is a variant of angioneurotic edema. Typically, it occurs in young females and is characterized by intermittent swelling of the eyelid, BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: A 6-year-old child presents for evaluation of a rapid onset of proptosis with lateral and downward displacement of left eye as shown. Biopsy reveals a pleomorphic rhabdomyosarcoma. With respect to frequency and prognosis, what characteristics does this type of rhabdomyosarcoma have relative to others?

options.A: 381c- 497c- It is most common, with the best prognosis.
options.B: It is least common, with the worst prognosis.
options.C: It is least common, with the best prognosis.
options.D: It is most common, with the worst prognosis.

explanation: This child has rhabdomyosarcoma, which is the most common orbital malignancy in childhood. Although onset can occur at any age, the average age at onset is 5 to 7 years, with the typical age at diagnosis being 7 to 8 years. Children with rhabdomyosarcoma have a history of the sudden onset and rapid evolution of proptosis. Periorbital ecchymosis may also be present. A history of trauma is often elicited, but trauma is frequent and misleading. Clinical features include unilateral proptosis, globe displacement, ptosis, and eyelid edema. Pain is uncommon (approximately 10% of cases). Prompt orbital biopsy is required for conﬁrmation of the diagnosis whenever rhabdomyosarcoma is suspected. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy should not be relied upon to make the diagnosis, because aggressive chemotherapy typically requires more deﬁnitive histologic conﬁrmation and this may delay a proper biopsy. Patient management involves a multidisciplinary approach. The 4 types of rhabdomyosarcoma are embryonal, botryoid, pleomorphic, and alveolar. Of these, pleomorphic is the least common, with the best prognosis. The embryonal is the most common type. The alveolar type is the most malignant. A mnemonic for these 3 is: "embryonal everyone, pleomorphic please, alveolar awful."

question: What is the cause of acute spastic entropion?

options.A: contracture of the tarsus and conjunctiva

explanation: Spastic entropion results from ocular irritation or inﬂammation. Contracture of the inner lamella can cause cicatricial entropion. Horizontal laxity of the eyelid, attenuation or disinsertion of eyelid retractors, and overriding by the preseptal orbicularis oculi muscle can result in involutional entropion. Congenital entropion can result from dysgenesis of the eyelid retractors.

question: When repairing a deep upper eyelid laceration with fat in the wound, it is generally advisable to avoid suturing what structure?
explanation: An upper eyelid laceration with fat in the wound describes an injury where the orbital septum is involved. The orbital septum arises from the periosteum over the superior and inferior orbital rims at the arcus marginalis. In the upper eyelid, the orbital septum fuses with the levator aponeurosis. When repairing such an injury, the levator muscle, levator aponeurosis, and tarsal plate should all be repaired. Suturing the orbital septum can lead to vertical shortening, with subsequent lagophthalmos and tethering of the lid to the superior orbital rim.

question: A 45-year-old woman has bilateral lower lid retraction and ectropion 1 year after cosmetic blepharoplasty. There is a vertical deﬁciency of anterior lamella of the lower lids. What procedure is preferred to treat the ectropion?
explanation: Reconstruction of the eyelid, whether necessitated by trauma or a surgical intervention, requires reestablishment of the lamellar planes. The eyelid has an anterior and posterior lamella, with the posterior lamella consisting of the conjunctiva, tarsus, and lower lid retractors. The anterior lamella consists of skin and muscle. With an anterior lamellar deﬁciency, the skin and muscle needs to be augmented. The most appropriate option is a full-thickness skin graft.

question: A 69-year-old woman presents with unilateral proptosis. Orbital ultrasonography reveals enlargement of the inferior rectus and medial rectus muscles with sparing of the muscle tendon. What associated examination ﬁnding would best support the ophthalmologist's working diagnosis?

options.A: optic nerve head pallor with retinochoroidal collateral vessels
options.C: pain on palpation of the inferior orbital fornix
options.D: salmon patch in the inferior conjunctival fornix

explanation: Upper eyelid retraction is the most common clinical feature of thyroid eye disease (Fig.1), being present either unilaterally or bilaterally in more than 90% of patients at some point in their clinical course. Conversely, thyroid eye disease is the most common cause of eyelid retraction. Restrictive myopathy is apparent in about 40% of patients. The combination of eyelid retraction and multiple enlarged extraocular muscles secures the diagnosis, even with normal thyroid function testing. In contrast to inﬂammatory myositis, imaging studies of the orbit will show fusiform enlargement with sparing of the muscle insertions into the globe (tendons). Of note, optic neuropathy from TED happens in 5% of patients from enlarged extraocular muscles at the orbital apex compressing the optic nerve. The orbital component of TED is not painful, unlike inﬂammatory orbital disease. A salmon patch in the fornix should prompt workup for localized spread of orbital lymphoma, which may be seen as a soft tissue mass on orbital ultrasound. Optic nerve head pallor with retinochoroidal collateral vessels is consistent with optic nerve sheath meningioma, which would not cause extraocular muscle enlargement. 3729- 4c3f- 85c4- c30735358270) .

question: A patient with thyroid-related orbitopathy that has been stable for 2 years presents to her ophthalmologist to request help in improving her cosmetic appearance. She has prominent bilateral proptosis and an obvious large-angle esotropia and lid retraction in her right eye. In what order should the surgeries applicable to her condition be performed?

options.A: Decompression surgery should be performed ﬁrst, then eyelid surgery, and then strabismus surgery.
options.B: Eyelid surgery should be performed ﬁrst, then decompression surgery, and then strabismus surgery.
options.C: The order does not necessarily matter; the most severe problem should be addressed ﬁrst.
options.D: Decompression surgery should be performed ﬁrst, then strabismus surgery, and then eyelid surgery.

explanation: As a general rule, surgery for thyroid eye disease should be delayed until the disease reaches a stable state for at least 6 to 9 months. Urgent surgery may be indicated when disease is so severe that the patient is at risk of compressive optic neuropathy or has severe corneal exposure refractory to medical management. When surgeries are undertaken, the order is very important. Orbital decompression procedures can alter the position of the globe and thus aﬀect extraocular motility; they should be done before strabismus surgery. It is important to note that a balanced decompression can help minimize a change in strabismus. question: What is a possible disadvantage of nonporous orbital implants?
explanation: Advantages of nonporous implants include a low rate of extrusion and cost-eﬀectiveness. Disadvantages of these implants include decreased motility, because there is only passive movement from the socket to the prosthesis. Implant migration in the socket may still occur. question: What is the most common cause of orbital cellulitis among adults?
explanation: Orbital cellulitis involves structures posterior to the orbital septum. It is most often due to secondary extension of acute or chronic bacterial sinusitis. Orbital cellulitis in adults usually involves multiple organisms, which can include gram-positive cocci as well as gram-negative bacteria such as H. inﬂuenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis, and anaerobes; therefore, broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy is recommended in these cases. Fungal infections occur in patients with predisposing factors, such as systemic disease with associated metabolic acidosis, diabetes mellitus, malignancies, and treatment with antimetabolites or steroids. Children are more likely to have orbital cellulitis caused by a single gram-positive organism. Trauma also can cause orbital cellulitis, which can be related to a foreign body or to an orbital fracture in a patient with pre- existing sinus disease. orbital exenteration.

question: What is the best management for most cases of primary sebaceous gland carcinoma? Haemophilus inﬂuenzae sinusitis B.
explanation: Management of sebaceous gland carcinoma includes excision of the lesion, with tumor-free margins. This procedure can be done with wide excision, frozen-sections, or Mohs micrographic surgery. Because of the nature of the malignancy, which may have skip lesions and pagetoid spread, map biopsies are also often done at the same time, to ensure that no residual tumor is left behind. Although adjunctive cryotherapy, radiotherapy, or chemotherapy may be considered, they are not used as primary therapy. Orbital exenteration is considered in the case of invasive or recurrent neoplasia and may be needed in cases of sebaceous cell carcinoma that are recurrent, large, or invade through the orbital septum.

question: What is the best next step in managing this patient's condition?

options.A: 5098- 4d95- Take him to the operating room for urgent debridement.
options.B: Start him on oral antibiotics and a course of steroids.
options.C: Defer further management pending biopsy results.
options.D: Start him immediately on intravenous antibiotics with a low threshold, and take him to the operating room if there is no improvement in 48 hours.

explanation: This patient has necrotizing fasciitis (NF). Note the focal dark areas of necrotic tissue and the widespread desquamation of the entire face, both of which are characteristic of NF. Mortality for NF is quite high. One study showed that overall mortality for NF is 28%, with a lower rate (10%) in cases of eyelid involvement only, and a higher rate in cases involving the lower face and neck (32%). Given the high mortality rate and the fact that NF patients can clinically decline very rapidly, all patients with NF should be admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) for monitoring, as opposed to a general medical ﬂoor. Although starting immediate broad spectrum antibiotics is a correct measure to take, plans to go to the OR should not be delayed to watch for improvement. Prompt surgical treatment is one of the most important factors to decrease mortality in NF. This patient should be taken to the operating room to debride necrotic tissue as expeditiously as possible (ideally within no more than a few hours of presentation). Group A beta hemolytic streptococcus is the usual culprit found to cause NF. The aggressive nature of NF is determined in large part by how invasive that particular strain of the bacteria is. Virulence factors for this bacteria include the M protein and pyrogenic exotoxins (not endotoxins). M protein is an antiphagocytic virulence factor that renders the bacteria resistant to attack by host leukocytes.

question: A patient with diﬀuse actinic changes and a history of renal transplantation presents with progressive external ophthalmoplegia and forehead numbness that has progressed over several months. What is the most likely diagnosis? 1 mm ptosis, poor levator function, persistence of ptosis with instillation of a drop of 2.5 phenylephrine hydrochloride C.

options.A: orbital spread of a bacterial sinusitis
options.B: perineural spread of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma

explanation: A perineural spread of a cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) along the facial sensory nerves into the skull base (orbital apex and cavernous sinus) should be suspected in any patient with actinic changes or a history of facial cutaneous malignancies who presents with progressive periocular sensory and motor changes. SCC has a propensity for sensory nerves, and it occurs much more frequently in individuals with chronic immunosuppression (eg, those who have undergone renal transplantation). Bacterial sinusitis typically occurs in a fulminant fashion, and orbital involvement usually manifests with external eyelid changes (eg, erythema, edema) and proptosis. However, more indolent fungal sinusitis, especially aspergillosis, may occur in a slowly progressive manner. Tolosa-Hunt syndrome is an ill- deﬁned cavernous sinus inﬂammation that presents with explosive pain and responds to systemic corticosteroids. It is a diagnosis of exclusion, because other pathologies may mimic its symptoms. Microvascular cranial neuropathy typically aﬀects only 1 cranial nerve and typically resolves within 100 days. It does not usually aﬀect sensory nerves.

question: What is the preferred surgical intervention for severe upper and lower canalicular obstruction?
explanation: Both dacryocystorhinostomy and balloon dacryocystoplasty require an intact canalicular system for success. Probing and dilation cannot be performed without patent canaliculi. The only widely accepted method to treat bicanalicular obstruction is to bypass the blockage with a conjunctivodacryocystorhinostomy (CDCR) and a Jones tube.

question: What orbital surgical space contains the ciliary ganglion?
explanation: The orbit comprises 5 surgical spaces: subperiosteal, sub-Tenon, extraconal, intraconal, and subarachnoid. The ciliary ganglion is found on the lateral surface of the optic nerve sheath, 1 centimeter anterior to the annulus of Zinn, in the orbital apex between the optic nerve and the lateral rectus muscle. Therefore, it is intraconal. The only structures found in the subarachnoid space of the orbit are the optic nerve and the central retinal artery/vein. Both the subperiosteal and sub-Tenon spaces contain no signiﬁcant structures, although a variety of vessels pierce and pass through them. Both of these locations represent potential dead spaces where ﬂuid may collect because of the loose BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: The anatomical fusion of the sheath of the inferior rectus and what 2 structures can lead to lower eyelid retraction following strabismus surgery?
explanation: The Lockwood ligament is the inferior equivalent to the Whitnall ligament of the superior lid. The Lockwood ligament arises from the fusion of the sheath of the inferior rectus muscle and the capsulopalpebral fascia (or inferior tarsal muscle), as well as the check ligaments of the medial and lateral recti. The Lockwood ligament, in addition to being fused with the capsulopalpebral fascia (inferior tarsal muscle), is also fused to the inferior rectus muscle sheath. Therefore, vertical strabismus surgery that recesses or advances the muscle can alter the lid position. The orbicularis muscle does not insert into the tarsus and therefore does not aﬀect lid position. The Whitnall ligament is in the upper lid. &

question: A 54-year-old non-smoking woman complains of 2 weeks of rapid-onset right-gaze pain, proptosis, and diplopia. Other than remission of breast carcinoma following mastectomy 5 years ago, her medical history is negative. The results of her thyroid function tests, including the thyroid- stimulating hormone (TSH) test, are normal. Orbital computed tomography (CT) scan reveals a 12 mm diameter irregular inﬁltrating mass within the body of the lateral rectus muscle. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The presence of pain, proptosis, and early ophthalmoplegia suggests the possibility of metastatic carcinoma. The most common primary source of orbital metastases in women is breast cancer, which may occur many years after the breast has been removed. The extraocular muscles are frequently involved because of their abundant blood supply. The irregular inﬁltrating mass noted on CT is most consistent with metastatic disease. Lymphoma does not typically cause pain. Cavernous hemangioma would be well-circumscribed on CT scan, and would not typically appear within an extraocular muscle. Graves orbitopathy typically causes fusiform enlargement of the extraocular muscles, sparing the tendon insertion.

question: A 42-year-old woman complains of eyelid asymmetry and has 2 mm of left upper lid ptosis. Her pupils, ocular motility, and levator function are normal. What clinical test would help conﬁrm whether she is a candidate for transconjunctival Müller muscle resection?
explanation: The patient likely has involutional ptosis, which could be treated via external levator advancement or transconjunctival Müller muscle resection. If instillation of 2.5% phenylephrine restores the normal position of the lid, it suggests the patient would respond favorably to transconjunctival Müller muscle resection. Edrophonium (Tensilon) testing and ice testing are useful to diagnose myasthenia gravis. Tropicamide does not have a role in this setting.

question: When dissecting anteriorly across the zygomatic arch from the upper to the lower face, what structure is at risk of injury?

options.A: temporal branch of the facial nerve
options.B: temporal branch of the angular nerve
options.C: temporal branch of the angular artery
options.D: temporal branch of the maxillary nerve

explanation: The temporal branch of the facial nerve crosses the zygomatic arch anteriorly. It is unsafe to dissect from the upper face to lower face across this region. The angular artery and nerve are closer to the nasojugal fold.

question: What is the most common form of basal cell carcinoma?
explanation: Nodular BCC is the most common form of basal cell carcinoma. It presents as a ﬁrm, raised, pearly nodule that may have telangiectasias and central ulceration. Morpheaform is less common and behaves more aggressively than the nodular form. Multicentric, or superﬁcial, BCC can silently spread across the eyelid margin and mimic blepharitis. Central ulceration is a classic feature of basal cell carcinoma, but it is not a speciﬁc type. BCC lesions are most often located on the lower lid, and are typically painless. Conjunctival extension can occur, but it is not a typical feature of basal cell carcinoma.

question: Six weeks after probing of the lacrimal system, the family of a 13-month-old child reports that she continues to tear. A review of the operative notes indicates that the ophthalmologist had diﬃculty passing the probe past the canaliculus and into the lacrimal sac. What might have occurred during the procedure?

options.B: reactive stenosis at the canalicular-sac junction

explanation: Pushing through a "soft stop" can create a false passage. In this case, the site of resistance is located along the canaliculus, which would suggest canalicular stenosis or obstruction. A "soft stop" is usually accompanied by a wrinkling of the overlying skin. If this is encountered, the probe should be removed, and passage should be attempted again with proper horizontal tension along the lid to prevent bunching of soft tissue in front of the probe tip. Successful probing through the canalicular system will lead to a "hard stop" as the tip encounters the medial wall of the lacrimal sac and lacrimal bone.

question: During the biopsy of a presumed lymphoma involving the conjunctiva, what should the pathologist ideally receive?
explanation: During the biopsy of a lymphoma, the pathologist should ideally receive fresh tissue to be sent for cytogenetic/gene rearrangement/immunohistochemical studies to look for polyclonality (benign lymphoid hyperplasia) or monoclonality (lymphoma). While the concept that polyclonality denotes benignity and monoclonality signiﬁes malignancy does not apply rigidly to ocular adnexal lymphoid lesions, it can be a useful prognostic tool. A portion of the tissue is later placed in a paraﬃn block for histologic sections. Conjunctival scraping is not indicated, electron microscopy is not performed routinely, and culture is not helpful.

question: For a 7-year-old child with orbital cellulitis, what would be the most likely characteristic of the causative source?
explanation: Most young children with orbital cellulitis have infections caused by a single aerobic pathogen. In the neonate, S aureus and gram- negative bacilli are most common. In older children and adults, S aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, and S pneumoniae are common etiologic agents. Concurrent infections with multiple pathogens, including gram-negative and anaerobic organisms, can occur in older or immunosuppressed patients. &

question: Failure of what embryonal developmental process results in microphthalmia with orbital cyst?
explanation: Microphthalmia with orbital cyst results from failure of the choroidal ﬁssure to close in the embryo. Craniofacial clefts occur as a result of a developmental arrest or mechanical disruption of development. Etiologic theories include a failure of neural crest cell migration and a failure of fusion or movement of facial processes. Anophthalmia occurs when the primary optic vesicle fails to grow out from the cerebral vesicle at the 2-mm stage of embryonic development. Consecutive anophthalmia is thought to result from a secondary degeneration of the optic vesicle. 5 Filter by 50 per pa.

question: What is one advantage of enucleation, compared with evisceration?

options.A: It will not expose an occult intraocular malignancy.
options.B: It has a lower rate of implant extrusion.
options.C: It is a technically easier procedure to perform.
options.D: It results in better implant motility.

explanation: It is likely that the biggest advantage of enucleation over evisceration is that it will not expose an occult intraocular malignancy or disseminate it into the orbit. Evisceration should never be performed without preoperative B-scan ultrasonography to eﬀectively rule out an intraocular mass. Neither computed tomography (CT) nor magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is as sensitive as B-scan in this regard. The possible increase in sympathetic ophthalmia (SO) rates following evisceration is controversial. Because of the rarity of SO, there is no large study proving the association between evisceration and SO. Evisceration is technically simpler to perform than enucleation, often requiring less intraoperative time and anesthesia.

question: What upper eyelid mass most commonly causes mechanical ptosis?
explanation: Ptosis can be classiﬁed by the cause: myogenic, aponeurotic, neurogenic, mechanical, or traumatic. Mechanical ptosis is caused by an eyelid mass or orbital mass that weighs down the upper eyelid. Causes include plexiform neuroma, hemangioma, chalazion, skin carcinoma, orbital mass, and postsurgical or post-traumatic edema. Of these sources, chalazia are the most commonly encountered and therefore are the most common cause of mechanical ptosis.

question: Pulsatile exophthalmos is most closely associated with what neuro- oculocutaneous disorder?
explanation: Orbital pulsations can occur in various situations and can often be divided, depending on the presence or absence of a bruit. With bruits, pulsations can be seen in carotid cavernous ﬁstulas, orbital arteriovenous ﬁstulas, and dural arteriovenous ﬁstulas. Without bruits, they can be found in meningoencephaloceles, neuroﬁbromatosis 1 (NF1), and in cases involving orbital roof defects, such as removal of the orbital roof. Sphenoid wing dysplasia or aplasia in NF1 is associated with this orbital ﬁnding. Patients with NF1 with pulsatile proptosis have sphenoid wing dysplasia or aplasia. Tuberous sclerosis, von Hippel-Lindau disease, and neuroﬁbromatosis type 2 are other neuro-oculocutaneous disorders (phakomatoses) but are not associated with pulsatile exophthalmos.

question: A 5-year-old boy presents for evaluation of unilateral tearing for the past 2 months. In what population would the dye disappearance test (DDT) be best used?
explanation: The dye disappearance test (DDT) is used to assess lacrimal drainage outﬂow. This is a very good test in children, as it does not require probing or irrigation of the drainage system. This test is especially useful in the analysis of unilateral epiphora. Fluorescein dye is placed in the conjunctival fornices of both eyes, and a cobalt blue light is used to evaluate the tear ﬁlm. Special attention is paid to the symmetry or asymmetry between the tear ﬁlms of both eyes. The tear ﬁlm is evaluated for 5 minutes. At this point, a well-functioning lacrimal BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: A patient with a history of eyelid cancer in the past now presents with ipsilateral forehead pain, diplopia, and ptosis. What condition is most likely responsible for these symptoms?
explanation: This patient presents with a classic "cavernous sinus syndrome" -- facial sensory changes (in this case limited to the ﬁrst division of the trigeminal nerve), diplopia, and ptosis. A history of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (SCCA) of the upper lid should immediately raise the strong probability that perineural spread of the tumor has occurred along the skull base. Cutaneous SCCA carcinoma has a propensity for spread along sensory nerves (and on occasion along the facial nerve). It is notorious for recurrence in this cryptic fashion, even with "clear margins" on initial extirpation. The sensory changes may precede other cranial neuropathy by weeks to months, and the symptoms are often misdiagnosed as a "pain syndrome" or trigeminal neuralgia. The aﬀected sensory nerve is usually enlarged and enhances on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), but these ﬁndings may be subtle and missed by the radiologist without a good clinical history. In many cases, no previous history of cutaneous SCCA is present, but the patient either has widespread actinic changes over the face (with an undiagnosed SCCA) or has undergone multiple sessions of cryotherapy or cautery of suspicious facial lesions without biopsy. Bowen disease is another name for squamous cell carcinoma in situ of the skin. In situ carcinomas are not metastatic and would not cause these symptoms. Basal cell carcinoma accounts for 90%-95% of malignant tumors of the eyelid. These tumors are locally invasive, with an incidence of orbital involvement in 2%-4% of cases, mostly in inadequately treated or neglected tumors. BCC does not spread by perineural invasion. Muir-Torre syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition of sebaceous tumors involving the gastrointestinal, endometrial, or urologic systems.

question: Three weeks ago, a 23-year-old man had blunt trauma to the left upper lid. Examination shows he has 3 mm of left ptosis, which does not change throughout the day. He also has an elevated lid crease and normal levator function, ocular motility, and pupillary responses. What is the most likely type of ptosis in this patient?
explanation: Aponeurotic ptosis occurs when levator muscle is disinserted from the tarsal plate attachment and can occur secondary to age-related dehiscence (most common) or, less commonly, from trauma or intraocular surgery. Characteristics of aponeurotic ptosis include normal levator function, higher than normal eyelid crease (high-riding levator aponeurosis), and eyelid droop on downward gaze. Mechanical ptosis is from mass eﬀect that weighs or pulls down the upper eyelid. Myogenic ptosis has absent upper lid crease and absent-to-poor levator function. When acquired, myogenic ptosis results from localized or diﬀuse muscular disease, such as muscular dystrophy, chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia, myasthenia gravis, or oculopharyngeal dystrophy. Neurogenic ptosis when acquired results BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: Keratoacanthoma is a variant of what other eyelid malignancy?
explanation: Keratoacanthomas (KAs) occur most commonly on facial skin as single, large, elevated growth with a central crater. There is usually a history of rapid growth over 4 to 8 weeks, and often a history of spontaneous BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: The risk of what condition is thought to be minimized by the enucleation of NLP (no light perception) eyes within 14 days of penetrating injury?
explanation: Immune system sensitization to choroidal antigens is less likely if the inciting tissues are removed within 14 days of exposure. Therefore, some recommend enucleation of NLP (no light perception) eyes within 2 weeks following visually unrecoverable penetrating ocular injury to prevent sympathetic ophthalmia. Proliferative vitreoretinopathy may BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What would be the preferred management for a large, ﬂat eyelid lesion with irregular borders and varied pigmentation?

options.B: total surgical excision with margin evaluation

explanation: The most likely diagnosis for this lesion is a melanoma. Lentigo maligna accounts for 90% of head and neck melanomas. Management consists of total surgical excision utilizing permanent sections to assure complete removal. Biopsy is not preferred for a ﬂat lesion and, if performed, would not be done on the margin, because the examiner BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: Extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma (EMZL, also termed mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue [MALT] lymphoma) of the gastrointestinal tract has been associated with what chronic infection?
explanation: Ocular adnexal lymphoma comprises approximately 6%–8% of orbital tumors. The vast majority are non-Hodgkin B-cell type with less than 3% T-cell types. Bilaterality is reported in 10%-20% of cases. The most common type is extranodal marginal zone lymphoma (EMZL), comprising 50%-90% of all cases of ocular adnexal lymphoma. H.

question: What is the preferred management for the abnormality seen in this asymptomatic 4-year-old girl?
explanation: The ﬁgure depicts a yellow lesion in the inferior temporal conjunctivae. This is a dermolipoma, a congenital choristoma. The lesion is typically asymptomatic but may cause astigmatism if it extends anteriorly. Given that the lesion can extend into the orbit and/or lacrimal gland, it is most often observed; indications for subtotal excision are a cosmetically unacceptable appearance, irritation, astigmatism, and anisometropic amblyopia. &

question: A 2-year-old child has a mass above the medial canthal tendon that has been increasing in size over the past several months. The mass is painless and was discovered incidentally during a routine eye examination. What is the recommended management?

options.C: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the skull base

explanation: The main concern in a patient presenting with a slowly progressive, superomedial (above the medial canthal tendon) orbital mass is an expanding skull base process. In children, this is typically due to encephalocele (inferior herniation of brain tissue), meningocele (herniation of the meninges), or meningoencephalocele (herniation of both); these lesions are especially common in congenital clefting syndromes. Dermoid cysts may also occur in this region. Dacryocystoceles often form below the medial canthal tendon, but if there is any concern for encephalocele, consider imaging before probing and irrigation. In adults, the most common cause is an expanding frontoethmoidal mucocele, which may have eroded through bone into the orbit and anterior cranial fossa (Fig. 1). It is crucial to obtain imaging of the area before proceeding with any type of surgical intervention in this clinical situation, in order to avoid any potential intracranial complications. In children, an MRI is preferred to computed tomography (CT) for 2 reasons: 1. It will provide better imaging of the skull base soft tissue than CT; 2. MRI avoids radiation exposure to a young child's brain. 51fb-4071- b38f- 53215dd286c6&t=636150118800000000) &

question: What is the goal of orbital decompression surgery for Graves disease-related ophthalmopathy (thyroid eye disease)?

options.B: reduction of stare from lid retraction
options.C: expansion of the orbital volume to accommodate enlarged extraocular muscles
options.D: improvement of ocular misalignment and diplopia

explanation: Orbital decompression often, and in particular in the chronic stage of thyroid eye disease, does not aﬀect the orbital inﬂammatory process or its sequelae but simply expands orbital volume for the large muscles. It often does not have any eﬀect on lid retraction, even when proptosis is reduced, and it can in fact exacerbate diplopia.

question: An 88-year-old woman presents with an enlarging fullness in the lateral portion of both upper eyelids. The ophthalmologist suspects that she has age-related prolapse of the lacrimal gland. To conﬁrm this suspicion, the ophthalmologist and the patient agree that a biopsy should be performed. What portion of the lacrimal gland should be biopsied?

options.A: palpebral lobe because the secretory ductules pass through the orbital lobe
options.B: orbital lobe, because the secretory ductules pass through the orbital lobe
options.C: orbital lobe, because the secretory ductules pass through the palpebral lobe
options.D: palpebral lobe, because this is the prolapsed lobe

explanation: The lacrimal gland is composed of a large orbital lobe and smaller palpebral lobe. The gland is found in the lacrimal fossa of the frontal bone and innervated by parasympathetic/sympathetic ﬁbers via the pterygopalatine ganglion. Sensory innervation is from the ophthalmic branch of cranial nerve V. Ducts from both lobes pass through the palpebral lobe and empty into the upper conjunctival fornix. For this BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What is the most appropriate surgical repair for severe lower lid cicatricial entropion with retraction?
explanation: When assessing eyelid malposition, it is important to determine the eyelid lamellae that are involved in the pathologic process. The anterior lamella includes the skin and orbicularis oculi muscle, and anterior lamella shortening results in ectropion. The posterior lamella is the conjunctiva and tarsus, and shortening of this lamella results in entropion. Scarring and ﬁbrosis are key factors that lead to either posterior or anterior lamellar deﬁciencies.

question: Over a 2-year interval, a patient's trichiasis of the left lower lid is treated 4 times with electrolysis and cryotherapy. For the past several months, his eye has become increasingly irritated. What possible sequela of treatment most likely explains these symptoms?
explanation: Trichiasis is an acquired misdirection of the eyelashes. Management options include mechanical epilation, electrolysis, radiofrequency, cryotherapy, argon therapy, or full-thickness pentagonal resection. Cicatricial entropion is caused by vertical tarsoconjunctival contracture and internal rotation of the eyelid margin, resulting in irritation of the globe. Traumatic scarring, such as that caused by electrolysis, radiofrequency, or cryotherapy burns from trichiasis treatment, can lead to cicatricial entropion. &

question: Necrotic-appearing tissue is found on the roof of the mouth of a 49- year-old patient with poorly controlled diabetes and orbital cellulitis. What infectious organism is the most concerning to the examining physician?
explanation: Necrotic-appearing tissue in the oropharynx or nose in a diabetic patient is highly suggestive of mucormycosis. Delayed diagnosis of mucormycosis could be lethal. Staphylococcus and Streptococcus organisms are a common cause of cellulitis in adults (usually BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: Over the past 5 years, a 60-year- old woman has had slowly worsening vision and increasing proptosis in her right eye. She reports no sudden changes or eye pain. Her visual acuity is 20/30 OD, with a right relative aﬀerent pupillary defect, and her right optic disc is mildly pale. Given the visual ﬁelds and imaging shown, what is the next step in managing this patient's condition?

options.A: 8d93- bf2cde3cfd67&t=63478047960000000 orbitotomy with surgical excision of the lesion

explanation: Patients with intraorbital or intracanalicular compressive lesions typically present with slowly progressive vision loss, a relative aﬀerent pupillary defect (RAPD), and monocular visual ﬁeld loss. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of this patient shows a well-encapsulated intraconal lesion compressing the right optic nerve. The next step in management would be orbitotomy with surgical excision of the lesion for both diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. This patient underwent endoscopic medial orbitotomy with tumor removal. The ﬁnal pathology results showed cavernous hemangioma. Cavernous hemangiomas are the most common benign neoplasm in the orbit in adults. Slowly progressive proptosis is usually the principal ﬁnding, although compressive optic neuropathy also can occur. Imaging typically demonstrates a homogeneously enhancing, well- encapsulated mass. Treatment is surgical excision, if the lesion is causing signiﬁcant proptosis, compromising vision (as in this case), or growing signiﬁcantly. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy may provide the diagnosis, but it would not relieve the compression and could potentially make a cavernous hemangioma bleed. Stereotactic radiation would not provide a tissue diagnosis and is not the typical treatment for cavernous hemangioma, which was the most likely diagnosis based on the MRI. Continued observation with annual examination is not appropriate, because there is progressive worsening of vision from compressive optic neuropathy.

question: A 17-year-old boy has a pigmented eyelid lesion. Complete excision of the lesion shows it to be an ephelis (freckle). How should the patient's follow-up be managed?

options.A: Return every 6 months for evaluation of recurrence.
options.B: Return every 12 months for evaluation for new lesions.
options.C: Return every 3 months for evaluation of new lesions.
options.D: Return for regular postoperative wound care only.

explanation: An ephelis, or a freckle, is a small, ﬂat, brown spot on the skin. Ephelides are on the basal layer of the epidermis, and the number of epidermal melanocytes is not increased, but they extrude more than the usual amount of pigment onto the epidermal basal cell layer. Once completely excised they do not return. No treatment is necessary other than sun protection. Therefore, follow-up should be for wound care only.

question: A 58-year-old woman presents to the oﬃce unhappy with the appearance of her eyelids. She wants her eyelids to appear more youthful. What would be the most appropriate surgical approach?

options.C: suturing of the sub-brow tissue to the frontal bone periosteum
options.D: resection of upper eyelid skin with advancement of the levator aponeurosis.

explanation: The ﬁgure shows a patient with dermatochalasis, mild brow ptosis on the left side, and blepharoptosis. Surgical treatment should be aimed to correct the dermatochalasis and ptosis. An upper blepharoplasty is the best surgical approach and includes the resection of upper eyelid skin, with varying amounts of orbicularis, and preaponeurotic fat resection. If there is concurrent ptosis, this can be addressed with the same anterior eyelid incision through advancement of the levator BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: How can congenital myogenic ptosis be distinguished from acquired aponeurotic ptosis?
explanation: Similar to acquired aponeurotic ptosis, congenital ptosis can present as severe ptosis, include an elevated eyelid crease, and be unilateral or bilateral. Patients with acquired aponeurotic ptosis have ptosis in all ﬁelds of gaze, while patients with congenital ptosis have eyelid lag on downgaze. Eyelid lag is present because the poorly developed and stiﬀ levator muscle limits the relaxation of the eyelid in downgaze. Absent eyelid crease can be present in either. That is why it cannot be used to distinguish between the two. &

question: What ﬁnding indicates that the orbital septum has been violated by a penetrating injury to the eyelids?

options.A: rounding of the medial canthus and telecanthus
options.B: presence of orbital fat in the wound
options.D: inability of the patient to close the eyelids fully

explanation: The orbital fat is located posterior to the orbital septum. The presence of fat following an injury indicates that the orbital septum has been violated. Excessive bleeding from the wound, inability of the patient to close the eyelids fully, and rounding of the medial canthus and telecanthus can occur independently and without involvement of the orbital septum.

question: A 25-year-old white woman is concerned about a 1.5-mm diameter, tan, ﬂat lesion on her lower eyelid. The lesion has been unchanged since birth and darkens with sun exposure. What is the recommended management of the lesion?

options.A: continued observation, and biopsy if there are any changes

explanation: The clinical description is consistent with benign ephelis (freckle). Ephelides arise from hyperpigmentation of the basal layer of the epidermis. The number of epidermal melanocytes is not increased, but they extrude more than the usual amount of pigment into the epidermal basal cell layer. These lesions are common in fair-skinned individuals and darken with sun exposure. No treatment is necessary other than sun protection. The patient should be reassured, although it is always prudent to consider biopsy if the lesion changes. Given the description of stable behavior of the ephelis, excision and/or biopsy is not appropriate at this time. &

question: When operating in the region of the temporal fossa, in what tissue layer is the temporal (frontal) branch of cranial nerve VII found?
explanation: In the temporal area, the temporal (frontal) branch of cranial nerve VII crosses the zygomatic arch and courses superomedially in the deep layers of the temporoparietal fascia (also called the superﬁcial temporalis fascia), often near branches of the temporal artery. question: A 34-year-old man has an esotropia of 30 PD in primary gaze, which increases in right and left gaze. Abduction and elevation are bilaterally reduced. He has right greater than left upper eyelid retraction. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation: This case describes esotropia and eyelid retraction in a young adult male, with both abduction and elevation deﬁcits. These ﬁndings are most likely due to thyroid eye disease. Early signs of thyroid eye BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What is the preferred technique for repair of a moderate (33 -50 ) defect of the lower eyelid?

options.C: primary lid margin closure with canthotomy and cantholysis

explanation: Repair of an eyelid defect depends on 2 main factors: the size of the defect and the age of the patient. In general, defects are easier to close in older individuals because of involutional soft tissue laxity of BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: In the emergency department following a motor vehicle accident, a patient has a normal globe examination and some periorbital ecchymosis, but no displacement of lateral canthus or malar ﬂattening. He denies any trismus. A computed tomography (CT) scan shows a nondisplaced zygomaticomaxillary complex (ZMC) fracture. What management is recommended?
explanation: A zygomaticomaxillary complex (ZMC) fracture (ie, malar complex fracture) is a relatively frequent midfacial fracture pattern that typically involves 3 facial buttresses: the zygoma (typically along the lateral orbital wall at the level of the frontozygomatic suture), the zygomatic arch, and either the medial or lateral malar buttress extending to involve the inferior orbital rim. Not infrequently, the orbital ﬂoor is also fractured. Clinical problems occur for patients if the fractured complex rotates. This typically results in inferior lateral canthal dystopia, a step- oﬀ deformity along the inferior orbital rim, malar ﬂattening, and trismus (limitation of mandibular opening from impingement on the muscles of mastication by the displaced zygomatic arch). Once enough rotation occurs, repair is indicated. However, observation is all that is needed in cases of nondisplaced or minimally displaced tripod fractures. High-dose corticosteroids are not indicated in facial fractures, especially if concomitant intracranial injury exists. In this case, there is minimal soft tissue edema, and even normal doses of steroids would provide little, if any, beneﬁt. It is also important to remember that displaced (rotated) ZMC fractures are notorious for "hiding" or minimizing the extent of the orbital ﬂoor defect, so the orbital ﬂoor fracture tends to look much smaller than it actually is. However, once the ZMC is rotated and plated back into its native position, the ﬂoor defect will open more widely, expanding the orbital volume and potentially causing posttraumatic enophthalmos or hypoglobus. It is therefore prudent to explore the orbital ﬂoor defect once the ZMC has been rotated back into normal position, and, as necessary, to repair the ﬂoor appropriately.

question: A patient with mild seventh nerve dysfunction that began immediately after acoustic neuroma removal now has tearing. What is the most likely cause?

options.C: aberrant regeneration of the seventh cranial nerve

explanation: The seventh cranial nerve is often damaged during removal of an acoustic neuroma, resulting in partial or complete paralysis of the ipsilateral facial muscles of expression. Orbicularis weakness interferes with the normal lacrimal pump function, causing epiphora. Recurrence of the tumor would not be expected to cause tearing. Aberrant regeneration of the seventh cranial nerve could cause hyperlacrimation, but this is much less common, and it would not be expected immediately after surgery. Nasolacrimal duct obstruction can cause tearing, but it is unrelated to the clinical scenario described.

question: A 35-year-old patient presents for follow-up after biopsy-proven lentigo simplex. How should the ophthalmologist respond to questions about the prognosis of the lesions?

options.A: Malignant transformation is more likely with childhood onset.
options.B: The lesions do not progress to melanoma.
options.C: Malignant transformation is more likely with adult onset.
options.D: The lesions often progress to melanoma.

explanation: Simple lentigines are ﬂat, pigmented spots larger in diameter than ephelides (freckles). They are benign and do not require treatment. Lentigo maligna is a diﬀerent skin disorder that confers a higher risk of malignant melanoma. Lentigo maligna lesions are characterized by irregular shape and uneven pigmentation in older persons.

question: What orbital disorder demonstrates a ﬂuid-ﬂuid level with neuroimaging?
explanation: Previously termed lymphangiomas, lymphatic malformations result from aberrant development and congenital malformation of vessels. The classic ﬂuid-ﬂuid level on orbital magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is seen with the so-called "chocolate cyst" of lymphatic malformations. Lymphatic malformations are relatively static lesions with very slow growth over time. The tumor becomes symptomatic when spontaneous bleeding occurs within its lymphatic channels, typically presenting as an acute orbitopathy. Bleeding sometimes occurs during or following upper respiratory infections and may be related to increased lymphocytic activity within the lesion, although this is admittedly conjecture. As the blood cyst matures and blood breakdown products form, a separation occurs between methemoglobin and deoxyhemoglobin as a ﬂuid-ﬂuid level that is best seen on MRI and is sometimes compared to the oil-vinegar line of salad dressing. Blood cysts are not a feature of the remaining lesions. Cavernous hemangioma usually demonstrates a heterogeneous uptake of contrast on MRI, but this is markedly distinct from the ﬂuid-ﬂuid line of lymphatic malformations.

question: What historical characteristic of a lacrimal gland tumor is most suggestive of adenoid cystic carcinoma?

options.D: persistence of symptoms for longer than 1 year

explanation: Adenoid cystic carcinoma is the most common malignant tumor of the lacrimal gland. This highly malignant tumor may cause pain because of perineural invasion and bone destruction. Proptosis, ptosis, and persistent symptoms for longer than 1 year are typical of the most common benign tumor of the lacrimal gland, pleomorphic adenoma.
